Supplementary diagnostics indicated that Harman’s first unrotated component accounted for 29.29% of the total variance, with no single factor dominating the measured covariance structure. In the composite OLS model, the highest VIF was 2.97 for consumer attitudes, followed by 2.07 for environmental values, with a mean VIF of 1.770. These values did not indicate severe conventional predictor collinearity. However, neither the single factor diagnostic nor the VIF results establish the absence of common-method bias. The HTMT assessment also identified substantial empirical overlap between consumer attitudes and purchase intention, requiring cautious interpretation of the estimated mediation relationships.

Figure 2 shows the importance-performance map for EV purchase intention. Consumer attitudes had the highest relative importance (0.477), followed by environmental values (0.358), acceleration (0.312), and policy incentives (0.308). Among these factors, acceleration had a comparatively lower performance score (57.824) than environmental values (61.947) and policy incentives (63.318). Driving range recorded the highest performance (69.136), despite its relatively low importance (0.087). Price similarly showed limited relative importance (0.071), alongside a performance score of 39.309. Charging time sensitivity recorded the lowest performance (25.677), although its importance was more modest (0.121). These results complement the structural model by distinguishing the relative importance of the examined factors from their reported performance levels.

Figure 2

5 Discussion

5.1 Economic evaluations

The price result is the clearest example of why conditional multivariate coefficients must be distinguished from unconditional consumer preference. A large body of EV research identifies high acquisition cost as a barrier, and the present data are consistent with that literature at the simple-association level where price was negatively related to purchase intention (Bansal et al., 2021; Egbue and Long, 2012; Larson et al., 2014; Noor et al., 2025; Rezvani et al., 2015). The sign became small and positive only after other economic, performance, environmental, and attitudinal variables were controlled. Such reversals can arise when correlated predictors share explanatory variance, producing a suppression or reversal pattern in the conditional coefficient (Tu et al., 2008). The findings should not be interpreted as evidence that Bahraini consumers prefer more expensive EVs or that acquisition price has ceased to be a barrier. The negative association in the simple model is consistent with the established literature on upfront cost, whereas the small positive coefficient in the full model represents a conditional relationship after adjustment for correlated economic, performance, environmental, and attitudinal factors. Price therefore remains a relevant structural constraint, even though its unique association changes once other adoption considerations are included.

This distinction also addresses the absence of significant attitudinal mediation for price. Price was not a significant predictor of attitude in the primary mediation model, and its indirect CI included zero. In a market with subsidized gasoline and low prior EV ownership, price may remain an important external sacrifice without being consistently absorbed into a generalized evaluation of EVs once perceived benefits, policy support, performance, environmental values, and attitude itself are modeled simultaneously (Bansal et al., 2021; Hasan et al., 2024; Kant et al., 2024; Lashari et al., 2021; Shareeda et al., 2021). Research increasingly shows that EV intention is “beyond the cost” in the sense that cost remains relevant but competes with infrastructure confidence, environmental benefit, policy expectations, and product attributes (Kim et al., 2025). The present result should be read in that conditional sense, not as evidence that cost ceases to matter.

Perceived economic benefits produced a different mechanism. The direct path to intention was insignificant, but the indirect path through attitude was significant. This is consistent with the distinction between immediate acquisition sacrifice and expected long-run value. Total cost advantages are prospective and cognitively evaluated, as consumers must believe that lower energy or maintenance costs make the EV a worthwhile proposition before those benefits translate into purchase intention (Liu et al., 2021; Palmer et al., 2018; Soszynska et al., 2024). The indirect-only pattern therefore supports an attitudinal internalization process similar to prior evidence on perceived value and EV adoption (Ali and Naushad, 2022; Dau et al., 2025; Higueras-Castillo et al., 2019). In Bahrain, this pathway is plausible because subsidized gasoline can reduce the immediate visibility of operating savings, making favorable interpretation of long-run economic value more important (Shareeda et al., 2021).

Policy incentives showed both a direct and indirect effect. This complementary pattern is consistent with research showing that incentives can alter the objective purchase environment while also improving perceived value, legitimacy, and feasibility (Bian and Panyagometh, 2023; Wang et al., 2021; Xue et al., 2023). Directly, financial or non-financial support can reduce cost and inconvenience. Indirectly, visible policy commitment can strengthen the consumer’s attitude toward EV adoption. Evidence from the U.S., Norway, Europe, China, and fleet adoption likewise suggests that incentive effects depend on design, market maturity, and the wider policy mix rather than on one universal subsidy coefficient (Alali et al., 2022; Jenn et al., 2018; Langbroek et al., 2016; Martins et al., 2024; Mersky et al., 2016; Zhao et al., 2024). For Bahrain, the finding implies that policy development may matter not only because an incentive changes private cost, but also because it can reshape confidence in the emerging EV ecosystem.

5.2 Functional-performance evaluations

Driving range illustrates a different form of conditionality. The simple relationship with purchase intention was positive and significant, consistent with decades of research showing that inadequate range and range anxiety can deter EV adoption (Egbue and Long, 2012; Kim et al., 2017; Neubauer and Wood, 2014). The coefficient remained positive in the performance domain model but became small and insignificant after the full set of correlated determinants was included. The appropriate conclusion is therefore not that driving range is irrelevant in Bahrain, but rather that range has clear lower-order relevance but contributes limited unique variance once acceleration, charging time sensitivity, economic evaluations, environmental values, and attitude are considered together. This is theoretically plausible because range is intertwined with charging access, travel needs, vehicle price, and broader perceptions of practical usability (Forsythe et al., 2023; Graham and Brungard, 2021). Bahrain’s compact geography may reduce the unique incremental value of additional range for routine travel, but that contextual interpretation must remain secondary to the empirical evidence of overlapping explanatory variance (Shareeda et al., 2021).

Acceleration showed one of the strongest direct effects and a significant indirect effect through attitude. This result supports the view that EV adoption is not solely a sacrifice-based environmental decision. Performance itself can create value, as the immediate torque and responsive acceleration provides a functional and experiential advantage, thus creating favorable driving experiences to drive positive attitudes toward EV technology (Bai and Zheng, 2020; Higueras-Castillo et al., 2019; Roberson and Helveston, 2020). Recent evidence that technological improvement is driving EV diffusion and that performance expectations matter in Oman further support the relevance of the result in the Bahraini context (Al-Maamari et al., 2025; Forsythe et al., 2023; Pamidimukkala et al., 2024). The partial mediation pattern suggests that acceleration has both an immediate product-attribute effect and an attitudinal route. Consumers may value responsive performance directly while also using it to form a more favorable overall evaluation of EV ownership.

The charging result requires careful interpretation in relation to the retained indicators. CT3 and CT4 assessed whether faster charging options and fast charging availability would encourage EV adoption, and as both items were reverse coded, higher scores indicated weaker endorsement of these charging improvements as adoption incentives. The positive direct and indirect relationships therefore suggest that respondents who placed less emphasis on these inducements also reported stronger purchase intentions and more favorable attitudes. This should not be interpreted as a preference for longer charging durations or as direct evidence of greater tolerance for charging delays. The finding remains relevant to Bahrain’s developing charging infrastructure, where convenience, charger accessibility, and uncertainty surrounding charging arrangements may shape consumer evaluations (Albinali et al., 2026; Cj et al., 2023; He et al., 2022; Qian and Yin, 2017).

5.3 Environmental values and the central role of attitude

Environmental values had significant direct and indirect effects, and the alternative bootstrap produced the largest indirect effect among the factors. This pattern is consistent with research showing that environmental orientation, green self-identity, and perceived ecological value can motivate EV adoption while also shaping favorable product attitudes (Barbarossa et al., 2017; Bouscasse et al., 2018; Degirmenci and Breitner, 2017; Rehman, 2025; Rezvani et al., 2015; White and Sintov, 2017). Value-attitude-behavior evidence likewise predicts that relatively enduring values become behaviorally relevant when they are translated into an object-specific evaluation (Dau et al., 2025). The direct effect suggests that environmental values retain motivational force beyond the generalized attitude measure, while the indirect effect shows that part of their influence is internalized into a favorable evaluation of EV purchase. In Bahrain, this dynamic is reinforced by increasing climate awareness and national commitments to carbon neutrality, with younger generations particularly receptive to sustainable mobility solutions (Alsabbagh and Alnaser, 2022; Shareeda et al., 2021). Cultural framing further shapes this relationship, as cross-country differences suggest that ecological responsibility is gradually becoming a social norm in Bahrain (Qian and Yin, 2017).

Consumer attitudes was the strongest direct predictor of purchase intention in the model. This is consistent with TPB and EV studies in which attitude is a proximal determinant of intention (Ajzen, 1991; Ali and Naushad, 2022; Gupta et al., 2024; Khurana et al., 2019; Kristiono et al., 2023; Wang et al., 2021). Recent research using TPB, TRA, TAM, and value-based frameworks likewise finds that attitude connects beliefs, perceived value, or environmental evaluations to EV intention (Chaturvedi et al., 2022; Rahma et al., 2024; Shalu and Pandey, 2025; Thwe et al., 2025; Udiyana and Yasa, 2025). However, the present mediation results refine this general proposition. Attitude was not a universal mechanism, as it provided indirect-only mediation for economic benefits, complementary partial mediation for policy incentives, acceleration, charging time sensitivity, and environmental values, and no significant mediation for price or driving range. This heterogeneity is theoretically meaningful because different factors enter the decision process in different ways.

The selective mediation pattern supports a more precise interpretation of integrated adoption models. Economic benefits appear to require evaluative internalization, whereas policy incentives, acceleration, environmental values, and charging tolerance have both attitudinal and non-attitudinal routes. By contrast, price and range show no significant specific indirect effects after the full model is estimated. This does not make them unimportant but indicates that their unique contribution to attitude is weak once overlapping determinants are controlled. Mediation theory explicitly allows such differences and cautions against classifying mechanisms solely from the significance of a direct effect (Zhao et al., 2010). The findings therefore support attitude as a central but context-dependent mechanism rather than a universal mediator applied mechanically to every EV determinant.

5.4 Theoretical implications

The first theoretical implication is that the contribution of an integrated EV adoption model should be judged by the mechanism it clarifies rather than by the novelty of a particular list of predictors. Economic, technological, social, environmental, and policy variables have already been combined in many forms across TPB, TAM, UTAUT, DOI, perceived value, and related models (Adnan et al., 2016; Bryła et al., 2023; Nazir and Tian, 2022; Rezvani et al., 2015). The present contribution is more specific, showing that the examined EV evaluations differ in their direct and indirect associations with purchase intention. The model shows empirically that the same mediator can be indirect-only for one factor, complementary for another, and absent for others. This pattern adds to the belief-attitude-intention literature by identifying where attitudinal mediation appears more or less prominent across the examined determinants.

Second, the disaggregation of performance matters, as range, acceleration, and charging time sensitivity are all performance variables that behave differently. Range had stronger lower-order relevance but weak unique full-model explanatory power, while acceleration retained strong direct and indirect paths, and charging time sensitivity showed significant direct and indirect effects once its orientation was interpreted correctly. Treating these attributes as a single performance construct would conceal these differences. The result supports more micro-theorizing about functional attributes in sustainable technology adoption (Forsythe et al., 2023; Higueras-Castillo et al., 2019).

Third, the study demonstrates the theoretical importance of distinguishing zero-order association from unique multivariate effect. The price sign reversal and weakening of range are not minor statistical details, but change the substantive claims that can legitimately be made. A coefficient in a multivariate structural model represents the predictor’s unique association conditional on the remaining model, not the consumer’s unconditional preference for the attribute. This distinction is especially important in integrated adoption models containing strongly related beliefs and evaluations (Tu et al., 2008). Robustness analysis should therefore be used not merely to confirm significance but to improve theoretical interpretation.

5.5 Policy and managerial implications

The results suggest that EV diffusion in Bahrain is unlikely to be accelerated by a single intervention. Policy incentives have both direct and attitudinal effects, indicating that a credible policy package can simultaneously improve purchasing conditions and consumer confidence. International evidence favors coordinated combinations of financial support, charging investments, and non-financial convenience rather than isolated measures (Anilan and Vij, 2024; Hardman, 2019; Qadir et al., 2024; Zhao et al., 2024). Bahrain’s emerging initiatives provide a foundation, but the policy environment remains less mature than leading EV markets (Bahrain Insurance Association, 2024; Bahrain News Agency, 2023). Any new incentives such as VAT exemptions, reductions in import tariffs, or priority parking and lanes should therefore be evaluated alongside infrastructure readiness, fiscal sustainability, and consumer awareness rather than treated as a stand-alone solution (Alsabbagh and Alnaser, 2022; Anilan and Vij, 2024; Shareeda et al., 2021).

For manufacturers and dealers, the findings argue against marketing EVs only as environmentally responsible products. Acceleration was a strong predictor, and environmental values also mattered directly and through attitude. Communications can therefore combine performance experience, credible cost of ownership information, and environmental value. Test drives may be particularly useful because direct experiences can correct misconceptions and make performance advantages tangible (Roberson and Helveston, 2020). Moreover, price communication must remain transparent, as the sign-reversal finding does not justify premium pricing as a demand strategy.

The IPMA findings provide further insight into the practical priorities emerging from the structural model. As Figure 2 shows, consumer attitudes, environmental values, acceleration, and policy incentives were among the most influential factors associated with purchase intention. Acceleration exhibited comparatively lower performance than other highly important constructs, suggesting opportunities for manufacturers and dealers to strengthen consumer awareness through practical demonstrations and test drives. Driving range, by contrast, showed the highest performance but relatively low importance. This pattern is consistent with its limited unique contribution in the full structural model and suggests that emphasizing longer driving ranges alone may offer less value than addressing broader consumer evaluations. In Bahrain’s compact geographic setting, communication focused on the adequacy of existing EV ranges for routine journeys may therefore be more useful than emphasizing maximum range specifications. Although charging time sensitivity showed the lowest performance, its reverse coded measurement and comparatively modest importance require cautious interpretation. Similarly, the low price performance score should not be interpreted as evidence that affordability is unimportant, particularly given the conditional nature of the estimated price coefficient. Overall, the findings support a coordinated approach combining policy support, performance communication, and improved consumer understanding of EV ownership.

Charging-related communication should also account for differences in consumers’ practical requirements. Potential adopters may be comfortable with home charging or short routine travel, whereas others require visible public fast-charging availability. Infrastructure planning in Manama and across Bahrain should therefore consider not only the number of chargers but also spatial access, waiting time, reliability, and expected demand (Albinali et al., 2026). Policy and industry actors can reduce uncertainty by publishing clear information on charger locations, charging times, installation options, and future network development.

Lastly, because 331 respondents were non-owners, the findings are especially relevant to pre-adoption communication. Prospective adopters may be evaluating EVs through incomplete information and imagined use rather than lived ownership experience. Evidence from non-user studies and policy research suggests that knowledge, trial experience, and credible information can influence adoption interest (Peng et al., 2025; Samarasinghe et al., 2024). Bahrain’s emerging market may therefore benefit from demonstration programs, fleet trials, public test driving events, and transparent total cost tools that allow consumer to evaluate EVs on practical rather than abstract terms.

5.6 Limitations and directions for future research

While this study provides important contributions, several limitations are acknowledged that shape the interpretation of the findings and point toward future research opportunities. First, the convenience sample does not provide known selection probabilities and cannot be assumed to represent the demographic or behavioral distribution of Bahrain’s population, all current vehicle buyers, or all potential EV adopters. The non-owner and demographic-control robustness analyses show that the main coefficient pattern is not driven solely by prior EV owners or the observed demographic composition, but these analyses do not convert a non-probability sample into a representative one. Future research should use probability-based or carefully stratified sampling where feasible and should compare Bahrain with other Gulf markets to determine which mechanisms are context-specific.

Second, the data are cross-sectional and self-reported. The temporal sequence implied by the theoretical model is grounded in prior theory but cannot be established causally from one survey wave. Common-method bias also cannot be eliminated completely when predictor, mediator, and outcome measures are collected from the same respondents at the same time. The Harman diagnostic did not indicate dominance by a single factor; however, this remains a limited assessment and cannot rule out common-method bias. Longitudinal, experimental, field, and simulation studies would provide stronger evidence on how attitudes and intentions change with policy interventions, test drives, ownership experience, or charging network expansion.

Third, policy incentives and driving range exhibited weaker internal consistency than conventionally preferred, with Cronbach’s alpha values of 0.621 and 0.532, respectively. Although both constructs met the commonly applied thresholds for composite reliability and AVE, the low alpha values introduce uncertainty into their measurement. Among the policy indicators, POL3, which concerns discouragement arising from insufficient financial support, had the lowest retained loading (0.653). For driving range, DR2 assessed range adequacy for daily needs with a comparatively low loading (0.617), while DR1 was excluded during measurement refinement. The retained range indicators also address different aspects of perceived adequacy, including daily travel, longer journeys, and comparison with conventional vehicles. These results do not establish that any single item caused the reliability problem, but they identify areas for further refinement. Future studies should use quantitative item development, cognitive pretesting, and additional scale validation to improve consistency while preserving the relevant dimensions of each construct.

Fourth, consumer attitudes and purchase intention were highly related, with HTMT = 0.933. The bootstrap CI [0.868, 0.990] excluded 1.00 but did not satisfy the stricter 0.90 criterion, leaving a substantive discriminant validity concern. This overlap is particularly relevant because attitude and purchase intention occupy separate theoretical positions in the proposed mediation framework. Although the constructs are conceptually distinguished, their empirical proximity introduces uncertainty into the interpretation of the estimated indirect relationships. Future research should develop more clearly differentiated attitude and intention measures, particularly by separating general evaluations of EV adoption from recommendation intentions and specific future purchasing commitments. Temporally separated measurement and observed adoption behavior would provide stronger evidence of the proposed distinction.

Fifth, the questionnaire measured EV perceptions at the general product-category level and did not anchor respondents to a standardized vehicle model, brand, price point, or segment. This was consistent with the study’s objective of examining general EV adoption beliefs, but it also means that respondents may have evaluated different internal reference vehicles when considering price, range, acceleration, charging requirements, and perceived value. Such reference-object heterogeneity may increase measurement variability and limit vehicle-specific interpretations of the findings. Future research can address this limitation through standardized vehicle profiles, experimental vignettes, stated-choice designs, or analyses stratified by vehicle class, price segment, or brand familiarity.

Lastly, the bounded theoretical model deliberately excludes variables such as perceived usefulness, perceived risk, trust, social influence, facilitating conditions, and environmental concern. This focus permits a clearer test of the economic-performance-environmental belief-attitude intention mechanism, but omitted constructs may explain additional variance or moderate the observed relationships (Acar and Taşkın, 2025; Nazir and Tian, 2022; Udiyana and Yasa, 2025). Future models can extend the framework in theoretically targeted ways rather than adding variables indiscriminately.

6 Conclusion

This study examined how economic, performance, and environmental evaluations shape EV purchase intention in Bahrain, with consumer attitudes modeled as a potential mediating mechanism within a PLS-SEM framework. The results show that attitude is central but not universal. Economic benefits operated primarily through attitude, while policy incentives, acceleration, charging time sensitivity and environmental values operated through both direct and indirect pathways, and price and driving range did not exhibit significant specific indirect effects through attitude. This determinant-specific pattern supports a selective mediation perspective in which different EV evaluations enter the decision process through different psychological routes.

The robustness analyses also materially refine the interpretation of the most unusual coefficients. Price was negatively related to intention in the simple model and became small and positive only after adjustment for correlated determinants, so the full-model coefficient cannot be interpreted as a preference for expensive EVs. Driving range was positively associated with intention but lost unique significance in the complete model, indicating overlapping rather than absent relevance. The positive charging coefficient reflects the reverse coded measurement of faster charging inducements and should not be interpreted as a preference for slower charging. These distinctions make the substantive conclusions more conservative and defensible.

For Bahrain, the findings indicate that EV diffusion will require a combination of policy credibility, performance experience, economic value communication, charging confidence, and environmental positioning. For theory, the study demonstrates that integrated adoption models are most informative when they explain how determinants operate rather than simply how many determinants are included. Future research should test these mechanisms with representative, longitudinal, experimental, and revealed-behavior designs across Bahrain and the Gulf.
